title: Amazon Mining Watch's convolutional-network detector maps gold-mining scars basin-wide; 496,000 ha of protected and Indigenous lands affected 2018–2025, with no documented enforcement action
summary: AI mining detector (Earth Genome, Amazon Conservation, Pulitzer Center) maps mining scars basin-wide; 496,000 ha in protected areas 2018–2025 reported Apr 2026; no attributable enforcement event.
account: Amazon Mining Watch is a public platform built by the Pulitzer Center's Rainforest Investigations Network, Amazon Conservation Association and Earth Genome. In its own words, it leverages artificial intelligence to map the impact of gold mining. Its code repository describes the detector as an ensemble of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) trained on hand-labeled Sentinel-2 patches. The detector is run over the 8.2 million km2 Amazon basin, with detections recomputed yearly for 2018–2025 and quarterly from 2025. The repository reports specificity 0.976 and sensitivity 0.991 on a Venezuelan geographic holdout for the cumulative 2024 detections. Mongabay reported on 24 April 2026, on the platform's quarterly report. That report found about 6,000 hectares of mining deforestation in protected areas and Indigenous territories in the last three months of 2025. It found 496,000 hectares affected between 2018 and 2025. The enforcement operations on record are documented by the same tool maker without any AI role. MAAP #104 (4 August 2019) attributes a 92% fall in gold-mining deforestation at La Pampa to Peru's Operation Mercury of February 2019. That analysis used satellite imagery (ESA, Maxar, Sentinel-1) with no mention of machine learning. No cited source documents an enforcement action taken on an Amazon Mining Watch detection.
purpose: Automated detection and mapping of artisanal gold-mining scars in satellite imagery. The users are journalists, researchers, civil society and policymakers. The mapping is the intended use.

Basin-wide statistics exist, but no enforcement or policy outcome is attributed to the tool in a cited source.

ai_role.statement: The AI system produces the maps and area statistics themselves. The makers' repository describes an ensemble of convolutional neural networks on Sentinel-2 patches, with reported holdout specificity 0.976 and sensitivity 0.991. Mongabay independently describes the platform as training AI algorithms to recognize mining scars. No cited source links a detection to an enforcement action. Mongabay remarks that the platform is useful for cross-border work, citing 2025 Brazil-Colombia operations on the Pure River. It does not state that those operations used its detections. MAAP's Operation Mercury analysis, by the same maker, used satellite imagery without machine learning.

fields.account: Amazon Mining Watch is a public platform built by the Pulitzer Center's Rainforest Investigations Network, Amazon Conservation Association and Earth Genome. In its own words, it leverages artificial intelligence to map the impact of gold mining. Its code repository describes the detector as an ensemble of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) trained on hand-labeled Sentinel-2 patches. The detector is run over the 8.2 million km2 Amazon basin, with detections recomputed yearly for 2018–2025 and quarterly from 2025. The repository reports specificity 0.976 and sensitivity 0.991 on a Venezuelan geographic holdout for the cumulative 2024 detections. Mongabay reported on 24 April 2026, on the platform's quarterly report. That report found about 6,000 hectares of mining deforestation in protected areas and Indigenous territories in the last three months of 2025. It found 496,000 hectares affected between 2018 and 2025. The enforcement operations on record are documented by the same tool maker without any AI role. MAAP #104 (4 August 2019) attributes a 92% fall in gold-mining deforestation at La Pampa to Peru's Operation Mercury of February 2019. That analysis used satellite imagery (ESA, Maxar, Sentinel-1) with no mention of machine learning. No cited source documents an enforcement action taken on an Amazon Mining Watch detection.

fields.title: Amazon Mining Watch's convolutional-network detector maps gold-mining scars basin-wide; 496,000 ha of protected and Indigenous lands affected 2018–2025, with no documented enforcement action
fields.headline: Amazon Mining Watch maps 496,000 ha of mining in protected areas

provenance.basis: Preserved from the existing AIBD record; external sources were not rechecked.
Deterministic content version assigned by the local migration.

fields.account: Amazon Mining Watch is a public platform built by the Pulitzer Center's Rainforest Investigations Network, Amazon Conservation Association and Earth Genome. In its own words, it leverages artificial intelligence to map the impact of gold mining. Its code repository describes the detector as an ensemble of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) trained on hand-labeled Sentinel-2 patches. The detector is run over the 8.2 million km2 Amazon basin, with detections recomputed yearly for 2018–2025 and quarterly from 2025. The repository reports specificity 0.976 and sensitivity 0.991 on a Venezuelan geographic holdout for the cumulative 2024 detections. Mongabay reported on 24 April 2026, on the platform's quarterly report. That report found about 6,000 hectares of mining deforestation in protected areas and Indigenous territories in the last three months of 2025. It found 496,000 hectares affected between 2018 and 2025. The enforcement operations on record are documented by the same tool maker without any AI role. MAAP #104 (4 August 2019) attributes a 92% fall in gold-mining deforestation at La Pampa to Peru's Operation Mercury of February 2019. That analysis used satellite imagery (ESA, Maxar, Sentinel-1) with no mention of machine learning. No cited source documents an enforcement action taken on an Amazon Mining Watch detection.

produced_by: Free Sentinel-2 imagery composited on Google Earth Engine
Hand-labeled training set of 23,463 patches built from earlier human surveys with journalists
Ensemble CNN detector run over the whole basin yearly and quarterly
Public release of detections and code for journalists and NGOs
must_hold: Cloud-free composites over the period monitored
Mining scars visually distinct from sandbars, braided rivers and aquaculture ponds
Continued labeling and corroboration across years to limit false detections
A user, agency or newsroom willing to act on detections, which no cited source documents
